fire.intro: The US wildfire season as a running database: year-to-date scale against the ten-year norm, the pace curve, a map of the season's largest incidents, and the incident register itself. Represented as stat-map-and-table rather than a percentile band — NIFC publishes a clean year-to-date-versus-average figure, so that is what this shows.
fire.note: National year-to-date fires and acres are read from NIFC's Incident Management Situation Report (SIT-209); the 10-year same-date average is NIFC's own comparison. The incident register is curated from NIFC, InciWeb, Cal Fire and state agencies. Run fetch_fire.py to refresh the stat and pace curve.

cumulative.desc: Cumulative acres burned in 2026 versus the 10-year average for the same calendar date, at NIFC reporting waypoints. 2026 has run above the norm all year, and the gap widened into the August peak.
cumulative.inference: Every waypoint sits above the ten-year line. 2026 opened at nearly double the average through spring, and although the average catches up through the summer ramp, the absolute gap widened to roughly three million acres by mid-August — the season crossed 7.2 million acres with the traditional peak still underway.

incidents.desc: The season's largest and most consequential incidents, February to August. Dot size on the map scales with acres; colour runs from red (active / low containment) to amber (contained).

fire.inference: Fire is the defining US hazard of 2026: an early, fast start (the Morrill and Ranger Road grass fires set records before spring) that never let up, a Northwest- and Rockies-centred August peak, and the national system at its highest readiness level. The register also carries the season's human cost — the Morrill Fire and the three firefighters lost on the Snyder Fire — that the aggregate acreage figure hides.
